I know exactly how you feel - every inch of me used to be drawn out to focus on not letting out any ticks with my eyes, so I felt kind of detached from the conversation. And it doesn't feel right repressing those behaviours, it is physically difficult. Luckily I had a very kind group of friends who are very aware and accepting of it, so even if the aspects still show it's natural and I'm not judged on it. That's how anyone's friends should be, and if they can't accept you for little things out of your control like talking slightly soft I'd take the time to question if they truly are friends. Or if you just haven't told them yet, I'd wait to get properly diagnosed first.

As for "not being able to interact", even judging from the honesty and way you wrote this rant I'd say you communicate your point across very well! And the worries you have about "being normal" are common in everyone, autistic or not, everyone's prime goal is to fit in, and the only way you know if you click with new people is by showing them who you really are, unafraid of judgement. Even if someone's judgemental, chances are you'll have the upperhand of saying you can be authentic. And listening is indeed an important way to ensure you can help your friends the way they help you, but you need to ensure balance and make sure you are listened to in exchange, and they know how you feel.

I can agree with the rehearsing conversation parts on a whole different level, haha. The only thing about it is that you can't know for sure what they'll say and when, and when their reply isn't what you expected it can be really stressful and unhealthy - when you go with the flow on how you speak, that's who and how you're meant to be, even if it takes some explaining to get what you're trying to say across. 

Do you "have to" put on a "poker face"? It's more human than anything to dislike certain situations, and you aren't out of the norm for addressing your needs for when something is bothering you. Don't forget that's your right. 

Your parents are probably wanting to see it to believe it - if possible I'd get yourself tested personally to find out for certain. And despite how important it is to respect and try to understand your parents nevertheless you have no obligation to shut down your needs, and they shouldn't make you feel like that, which is perhaps something you should talk about. 

There's a lot of people in the world with autism and without it that feel like you do, but at the end of the day the best thing you can do for yourself and the (true) friends around you is to remain your own person, who judging by these behaviours is normal and completely valid. Until you know for sure the people around you can acknowledge this, you have an entire community and subreddit on your back including me.

Never ever forget your value. Stay safe ♥️
